content: The described approach and its potential refinements are still under validation and may require further adjustments. If the survey employs sampling designs other than Respondent-Driven Sampling (RDS), this method may not be appropriate. Recently, Dombrowski et al. utilized a one-sample capture-recapture (CRC) method entirely within a biobehavioral survey (BBS). This innovative approach involved a network-based variant of CRC, ensuring participant anonymity. It required sampling from each participant’s network connections and matching these connections against other participants in the sample and their respective contact lists. The initial capture was conducted using RDS via an online platform (e.g., Craigslist), while the second capture was based on respondents’ personal network connections. Recapture sampling relied on links to other participants derived from demographic data and an anonymized version of telephone numbers, referred to as telefunken matching. This technique allowed for population size estimation without the need to physically recruit a second sample. When considering population size estimation methods, it is important to recognize that all methods have limitations. Estimates are inherently uncertain, and different methods may yield varying results. Factors contributing to uncertainty include variability in the quality of service data (multiplier method), challenges in meeting assumptions (CRC), and transmission errors (Network Scale-Up Method, NSUM). Using multiple methods for population size estimation is recommended, as it provides checks, balances, and cross-validation. When different methods produce estimates within a similar range, confidence in the results is generally higher than relying on a single method. The choice of method and the number of methods used often depend on available resources. Those planning and implementing size estimation activities should consider integrating multiple methods when designing BBS or other surveys. Formative assessments, including social and geographic mapping and ethnographic observations, should be conducted before implementing a BBS. These assessments can help estimate the size of the population accessible at specific sites. If a household survey is planned, investigators should explore the feasibility of using NSUM to estimate the size of multiple key populations. Proper planning and preparation are critical before integrating any specific method into a BBS. When planning a BBS, it is essential to evaluate available resources and capacities to determine which methods can be integrated. For example, when using a service multiplier, it is important to assess the type, quality, and accessibility of service data, as well as any legal or other constraints. Formative assessments involving key population members can clarify the social and geographic distribution of the target population and the likelihood of reaching them. Engaging with target population members can also inform the selection of the most appropriate methods. Local estimates derived from BBS cannot be generalized as national estimates. For national-level estimates, data triangulation, projections, or methods like NSUM are required. High mobility within the target population may complicate census and enumeration efforts and violate CRC assumptions. Financial and technical resources also play a role in method selection. Census and enumeration are resource-intensive, while Bayesian statistics applied to RDS data require minimal additional time but demand technical expertise. CRC may require more resources and technical capacity compared to census and enumeration. Service provision tailored to the target population can facilitate the use of the multiplier method, provided reliable service data is available. CRC relies on several assumptions and works best when the target population is accessible and visible. It can be conducted as part of a survey or independently. The multiplier method is suitable when service providers can accurately count target population members and when the characteristics of the clientele align with the eligibility criteria of the BBS. Qualitative studies complement BBS by providing insights into behaviors and their underlying meanings. These studies can be conducted before, during, or after a BBS. Formative assessments help plan the BBS, while supplemental qualitative studies address additional questions raised during the survey. Together, quantitative and qualitative methods offer a deeper understanding of knowledge, behaviors, and practices, including how individuals and communities perceive HIV, sex, and drug use. Semi-structured interviews and focus groups are commonly used qualitative data collection methods. Semi-structured interviews involve open-ended questions, allowing for in-depth exploration of topics and follow-up questions. These interviews are often conducted with key informants, who provide valuable information for designing the BBS. Focus groups, on the other hand, are semi-structured group discussions that gather diverse viewpoints quickly. They are particularly useful for topics that do not require sharing private information. Combining semi-structured interviews and focus groups accelerates data collection and enables comparison of responses from different settings. When conducting qualitative studies, it is important to consider the cultural and gender aspects of interviewer selection. Peer-matched or gender-matched interviewers may help participants feel more comfortable. Ethical considerations, such as obtaining consent for audio recording and ensuring data security, must be addressed. Key informants should represent diverse perspectives to capture a broad range of viewpoints. For example, in a BBS among men who have sex with men (MSM), informants should vary in terms of age, socioeconomic status, education, HIV status, and sexual identity. Building trust with the target population through key contacts and venue visits is crucial for successful formative assessments and surveys. Focus groups are typically conducted with members of the target population and may require separate groups for subpopulations to understand their unique perspectives. For example, subgroups might include brothel-based and street-based sex workers or younger and older MSM. Using a combination of interviews and focus groups allows for a comprehensive understanding of the target population. In summary, population size estimation methods, qualitative studies, and supplemental data collection approaches are essential components of effective BBS planning and implementation. These methods provide critical insights into the behaviors, needs, and vulnerabilities of key populations, enabling the design of targeted interventions to address public health challenges.
